title: Andouille Po Boy Rolls for the Crew
displayTitle: Andouille Po Boy Rolls for the Crew
seoTitle: Andouille Po Boy Rolls for the Crew | Firehall BBQ
shortDescription: Po' boy night—butterflied andouille, rested remoulade, dressed New Orleans style
subtitle: Grilled andouille, remoulade, and crisp-toasted baguette for the crew
description: Butterflied andouille grilled cut-side down at 400°F for a mahogany crust, sliced into planks, and built dressed — remoulade, salted tomatoes, shredded romaine, pickle chips — on butter-toasted baguette.
equipment: Flat-top griddle or large cast-iron pan

steps.title: Whisk the remoulade first
steps.instruction: Whisk the mayonnaise, creole mustard, hot sauce, minced celery, sliced scallions, and smoked paprika, then chill at least 30 minutes — the rest is what blooms the mustard and paprika into the mayonnaise. It should bite back a little on a test cracker. This sauce carries the whole sandwich, so make it before anything touches the fire.

steps.title: Butterfly the andouille
steps.instruction: Split each andouille link lengthwise, stopping just short of all the way through, so it opens like a book and lies flat. Flat links mean double the crusty surface and nothing rolling around between the grates. Cut them cold straight from the fridge — a chilled casing slices clean instead of tearing.

steps.title: Settle the grill at 400°F
steps.instruction: Preheat to a steady medium, 400°F, and give it a full 8 minutes to even out. Andouille is heavily seasoned and fatty — a raging fire splits the casings and torches the drippings into an acrid haze before the inside is hot. Medium heat builds crust while the fat renders gently.

steps.title: Grill the andouille cut-side down
steps.instruction: Lay the butterflied links cut-side down and leave them 5 minutes until the face turns deep mahogany with crisp, lacy edges, then flip for 5–7 more. Andouille arrives smoked and pre-cooked, but you're after two things: real crust and real temperature — 160°F on an instant-read so the center is steaming hot, not just warmed at the surface.

steps.title: Slice the sausage into planks
steps.instruction: Slice the grilled links on a hard bias into long planks that blanket the bread edge to edge, and hold them covered in hotel pans at 140°F or above. Bias planks stay put under the toppings; round coins shoot out the back of the roll with every bite.

steps.title: Butter and toast the baguettes
steps.instruction: Split the french baguettes into 8 rolls, butter the cut faces, and toast on the flat-top at 375°F for 2–3 minutes until the faces are golden and crisp while the crumb still gives. A real po' boy crust shatters, then the bread yields — rolls toasted rock-hard shred the roof of your mouth.

steps.title: Stage the cold dressings
steps.instruction: Shred the romaine fine — po' boys take thin shreds that catch sauce, not leafy chunks. Slice the tomatoes 1/4 inch thick and hit them with a pinch of salt 10 minutes ahead so they actually taste like tomatoes. Drain the pickle chips well; wet toppings soak the roll before it leaves the counter. Keep it all cold until the build.

steps.title: Build them dressed
steps.instruction: Swipe remoulade generously on both toasted faces, then layer sausage planks, salted tomato slices, shredded romaine, and pickle chips. In New Orleans this is ordered 'dressed' — cold crunch against hot, smoky, spicy links is the entire point of the sandwich. Wrap each one in parchment; it holds the build together and catches the drips.

steps.title: Hold for call interruptions
steps.instruction: If tones drop mid-cook: turn off direct heat and cover grilled andouille — hold at 140°F in a warm cabinet or 200°F oven, never below 140°F for more than 30 minutes cumulative. Log hold time on the pan with a grease pencil. If tones drop after service, cover hot food and keep sides on low heat or ice as appropriate. On return, spot-check proteins at safe internal temp before reopening the line.

steps.title: Pack down leftovers safely
steps.instruction: Cool grilled andouille and hot components in shallow hotel pans within two hours — deep pots stay in the danger zone too long. Label with date; reheat proteins to 165°F minimum before second shift. Store cold components separately so textures survive overnight.

proTips: Butterfly, don't halve — the hinge keeps each link in one piece and doubles the crusty surface.
Remoulade needs its 30-minute rest; whisked and served straight away it just tastes like spicy mayonnaise.
Salt the tomatoes and drain the pickles ahead — wet toppings are how a po' boy roll dies young.
Keep a backup tray at 200°F for firefighters returning from a run — never serve picked-over pans to late crew.
Taste for salt at the end — hall palates run salty after long shifts.
Log hold times on the pan with a grease pencil when tones drop mid-service.
Spot-check proteins with an instant-read thermometer before reopening the line after a call.
tonightSpread: Main: Grilled andouille po' boys, dressed
Sides: pickle chips, kettle chips or red beans and rice
Set hot components closest to the crew; cold crunch and toppings at the far end of the line.
Keep a backup tray at 200°F for firefighters returning from a run.
leftovers: Cool grilled andouille in shallow pans within two hours; label with date and reheat to 165°F before second shift.
Store cold sides separately — hot and cold stacked overnight ruins texture.
Day-two andouille slices straight into jambalaya, red beans, or a breakfast scramble.
Keep rolls and fixings apart overnight — a built po' boy in the fridge turns into bread pudding.
whyCrewsLikeIt: Smoky, spicy links with a crackling toasted roll and a remoulade that bites back — a sandwich night that eats like a trip to New Orleans instead of another pulled pork repeat.
mealPrepNotes: Make the remoulade and stage the cold toppings ahead. Butterfly and cook the links at 400°F to 160°F, hold planks at 140°F or above up to 40 minutes, and toast rolls in batches right before the build.
substitutions: Smoked kielbasa swaps for andouille when the store is out — it runs milder, so double the hot sauce in the remoulade.
No creole mustard? Whole-grain mustard plus a dash of hot sauce lands close.
Soft hoagie rolls work if real baguette is too crusty for the crew — toast them a minute less.
Shredded iceberg stands in for romaine and holds crunch even longer against the hot filling.
